wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.rappels: One to three short single-rope rappels off natural anchors down the south gullies to the Eye Col; parties continuing to West Twin Needle exit by the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch on two double-rope rappels
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.rappel_count_note: Reversing the route takes one to three short single-rope rappels off horns and slings, depending on snow cover and the gully taken; their positions are not published. Two 60 m ropes are recommended because the enchainment exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch needs two double-rope rappels.
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.descent_text: Most parties reverse the route: downclimb the south-facing gullies back to the Eye Col and continue down into Crescent Creek Basin, a mix of class 4 downclimbing and short rappels off natural anchors (rock horns and slings - no bolted stations reported) on loose rock; expect 1-3 short single-rope rappels depending on snow coverage and the exact gully taken. East Twin Needle is frequently climbed in combination with West Twin Needle as part of a Southern Pickets enchainment; in that case parties continue the ridge west and exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch rather than re-descending the Eye Col gullies. That exit is better documented: two rappels using double 60m ropes are needed below the notch to get past vertical slabs, landing on grass and sloping rock around 6,800'; from there the route continues down a south gully with additional short rappels over vertical rock above a lingering snowfield before regaining Crescent Creek Basin. All anchors encountered on this descent are natural (horns, chockstones, slings) - carry cord/webbing for anchor building and expect to leave gear. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: back up and over the Chopping Block ridge, down The Barrier (roughly 4,300' of descent to Terror Creek - loose and brushy, arguably harder in descent than ascent), across Terror Creek, and out the Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.

rappel_detail.pull: Five single-rope rappels totalling roughly 400 ft, so a 60 m rope doubled covers every one — two ropes buy nothing here.
rappel_detail.notes: First of three rappels heading northeast from the summit area.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural anchor (slung horn/block), trending NE off summit
hazards: Easy to rappel past the next anchor: it appears short of the rope end and does not read as a station from above
Parties have had to free a jammed rappel rope on this descent, and one needed a handline thrown down to finish the exit gully
rappel_detail.station: A slung horn at the summit. The line drops straight down the northeast face rather than following any rib or ridge, and the stations below are oddly rigged and scruffy rather than obvious — they come into view before you reach the end of a 60 m rope, not at it.

rappel_detail.notes: Second of the three NE-trending rappels.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural/tat anchor, continuing NE trend

rappel_detail.notes: Third rappel; followed by a short, exposed grassy traverse east to the next rock rib before the final two rappels.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural/tat anchor near next rock rib
hazards: The link between the two anchors is a sloping grass-and-dirt traverse over slab with full exposure, and it is the section parties are usually unroped on
rappel_detail.station: The third rappel ends at the start of a short, exposed grassy traverse running east to the next rock rib. The following anchor is on that rib, not beneath you, so you walk before you rappel again.

rappel_detail.notes: First of two rappels dropping onto the East Ledges; a handful of fixed/bolted stations exist along this option.
rappel_detail.anchor: Mixed natural/fixed anchor above East Ledges

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel reaching the East Ledges, from which loose class 3-4 ledges/slabs are descended on foot above the Boston Glacier.
rappel_detail.anchor: Anchor above East Ledges
hazards: Several hundred metres of loose sandy and grassy 3rd-class ledges follow, with 4th-class steps where the ledges cross each rock rib
Cairns come in a higher and a lower set at every rib and the two are not equivalent — the low line finishes in a 4th-class red gully
Rockfall onto your own party on the ledges and the slabs below: move one at a time between sheltered stances
rappel_detail.station: The last rappel lands on the East Ledges themselves. Some parties instead downclimb from the bottom of this rope to a further anchor on steep ledges above the Boston Glacier rather than walking straight off.

Individual lengths are not stated, so no per-station length is shown.

wa_forbidden_peak_east_ridge.rappels: ~5 single-rope rappels down the north side on the East Ledges descent, the standard way off this route. Reversing to the West Ridge instead takes about eight.

These stations are the East Ledges descent: three rappels heading northeast from the summit, a short exposed grassy traverse, then two more onto the ledges. Individual lengths are not stated, so no per-station length is shown.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 3 on a single rope, down pitch 3 to the anchor at the top of pitch 2.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted belay anchor
rappel_detail.station: The anchor at the top of pitch 3.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 3 on a single rope, down pitch 2 to the anchor at the top of pitch 1.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted belay anchor
rappel_detail.station: The anchor at the top of pitch 2.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 3 on a single rope, down pitch 1 to the ground.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted belay anchor

wa_davis_holland_route.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels from the bolted belays, starting at the top of pitch 3; double ropes make it one long rappel to the ground
wa_davis_holland_route.rappel_count_note: Every belay is bolted. Most parties rappel from the top of pitch 3 rather than continuing up the brushy upper pitches. With two ropes it is one long rappel to the ground; with a single rope, one per pitch.
wa_davis_holland_route.descent_text: Most parties rappel from the bolted anchor at the top of pitch 3 rather than continuing up the brushy upper pitches or onto Lovin' Arms. Every belay on the route is bolted. Double ropes allow a long rappel to the ground; with a single rope, expect more, shorter rappels.

wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.rappels: Counts for this rappel line differ - about 20 to 25 double-rope rappels off the chained stations, interspersed with downclimbing. They do not correspond one-to-one with the route's 23 pitches. Two 60 m ropes are required; a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for some stations. Reported rappel times run 2.5 to 4 hours.
wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.descent_text: Rappel the line. Two 60 m ropes are required — a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for some stations. Reported rappel times run 2.5 to 4 hours. The stations are chained; one station 10 m above the crux anchor lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of the crux pitch in one rappel. Carrying over the top and descending the far side of the mountain has been done but risks an extra night out in brushy, cliffy terrain, and is not recommended. Knot your rope ends: a climber died here on September 7, 2014 after deliberately bypassing a station in fading light, running out of rope, and falling roughly three pitches. Start the rappels with real daylight in hand, and watch for parties still climbing beneath you.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 8, single rope, to the col at the top of #2 Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: anchor at the top of the easy summit slab
rappel_detail.station: From the summit, scramble down to the top of the easy slab.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 8, the first of about four double-rope rappels (two 60 m ropes) down #2 Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted rappel station
rappel_detail.station: Scramble from the col to the bolted station on the east side of #2 Gully.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 8, double-rope, down #2 Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree or chockstone with old slings
hazards: Slings here date back decades; back them up or replace them.
rappel_detail.station: After traversing a long stretch of slab, up to 100 yards, on the east side of the gully.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 4 of 8, double-rope, down #2 Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree or chockstone with old slings
rappel_detail.station: The next station down the east side of the gully, after another slab traverse.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 5 of 8, double-rope. Near the base of the gully, pack the ropes and downclimb.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree or chockstone with old slings
hazards: The west-side rock near the base of the gully is the loosest on the descent; a party member was struck by a 500 lb block that came loose under hand pressure in 2001.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 6 of 8, single rope, off the steep part of the ramp. Continue down past the Glade Saddle.

rappel_detail.station: The steep section of the wooded ramp, reached after crossing back over the Y Notch and the Key Ledge Traverse.

rappel_detail.station: The top of the lower slab.

wa_garfield_mountain_south_route.rappels: About 8 rappels: one single-rope from the summit slab to the col, about four double-rope (two 60 m ropes) down #2 Gully, one single-rope off the wooded ramp, and two double-rope down the lower slab
wa_garfield_mountain_south_route.descent_text: From the summit scramble down to the top of the easy slab and rig a single-rope rappel to the col at the top of #2 Gully. From there scramble to a bolted rappel station and make the first of about four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes, traversing 100-yard stretches of slab between stations on the east side of the gully; the lower stations are on trees and chockstones with slings dating back to the 1990s. Pack the ropes near the base of the gully and downclimb — this is where the west-side rock is loosest and where a party member was struck by a 500-pound block that cut loose under hand pressure in 2001. Cross back over the Y Notch and the Key Ledge Traverse, make a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, and continue down past the Glade Saddle. Two more double-rope rappels land you at the base of the slab at 2,900 ft; from there it is the wooded ridge, then the dirt gully to the creek at 2,100 ft, then the faint trail and the dry creek bed to the car. Expect to lose the trail in the dark at least once.
